industries.name: Auto and manufacturing
industries.overview: India builds and sells vehicles at record scale, from two-wheelers to commercial trucks, and a large component industry feeds the vehicle makers. It matters because it is one of the biggest parts of Indian manufacturing, and it ties together steel, electronics, rubber and logistics.

policies.name: PLI scheme for automobiles and auto components
policies.what: Pays incentives on sales of advanced automotive technology products made in India. Outlay ₹25,938 crore; 82 approved applicants (30 Nov 2025); ₹1,350.83 crore paid to five applicants; sales of ₹32,879 crore achieved by 30 Sep 2025 against an eligible-sales target of ₹2,31,500 crore until March 2028.
policies.sourceName: Ministry of Heavy Industries, on PIB

policies.name: PM E-DRIVE
policies.what: Electric vehicle demand incentives, e-buses and public charging. Launched September 2024, extended to 31 March 2028. Outlay ₹11,900 crore (see conflicts). 26.59 lakh EVs sold as of June 2026 against an incentive-supported target of about 28.30 lakh. ₹4,391 crore for 14,028 e-buses; ₹2,000 crore earmarked for charging.
policies.sourceName: Government factsheet, as reported by DD News

policies.name: Wider manufacturing push
policies.what: The government lists PLI schemes, PM GatiShakti, the National Logistics Policy and BHAVYA among its measures to strengthen manufacturing and diversify supply chains.
policies.sourceName: Lok Sabha reply, as reported by ANI

policies.name: Vision 2030 (NITI Aayog)
policies.what: Goal of US$145 billion in production, US$60 billion in exports, and a rise in India's global component trade share from 3% to 8%.

drivers: Record domestic demand: all four vehicle segments hit their highest-ever sales in FY2025-26 (SIAM).
Exports are rising fast: passenger +17.5%, two-wheelers +23.4%, three-wheelers +50.1% (SIAM).
Policy support through PLI and PM E-DRIVE, which together channel crores into manufacturing and EVs.
EV adoption: 26.59 lakh EVs sold under PM E-DRIVE as of June 2026.
Localisation: the PLI scheme requires domestic value addition, which pushes more of the EV supply chain to be built in India (PIB).

players.structure: A few large vehicle makers buy from a very large component base: component makers supplied ₹6,62,893 crore to vehicle makers in FY2025-26 (ACMA). The names below are approved PLI applicants, not a ranking by size.

challenges: Component trade gap: imports (US$25.4 billion) exceeded exports (US$24 billion) in FY2025-26 (ACMA).
India holds only about 3% of globally traded auto components, so most of the global component trade is elsewhere (NITI Aayog).
PLI progress is slow so far: ₹1,350.83 crore disbursed against a ₹25,938 crore outlay, and ₹32,879 crore of sales against a ₹2,31,500 crore target (PIB).
Manufacturing's share of GVA is flat at 14.8% (14.7% in 2022-23) despite 10.7% growth (Lok Sabha reply).
ACMA lists geopolitical developments, supply chain disruptions and raw material volatility as risks to watch.
opsAngle: Component supply moves with vehicle output: OEM supplies rose 16.3% to ₹6,62,893 crore, so capacity, inventory and delivery frequency at suppliers have to scale with record vehicle volumes.

Sourcing and localisation: imports exceed exports in components, and the PLI's domestic value addition rule pushes makers to localise parts. Expect questions on make-versus-buy and supplier development.

Export-readiness: vehicle exports are growing fast, yet India's share of traded components is about 3%, so quality, cost and delivery performance are what decide whether more of that trade can be won.
gdQuestions: India's component imports are higher than exports: is localisation the answer, and what would it cost?
Record vehicle sales but a flat manufacturing share of GVA: is auto really lifting Indian manufacturing?
Should the government keep paying PLI incentives when disbursement is this slow?
conflicts: NITI Aayog summary on PIB: one line says the auto sector gives 7.1% of 'global GDP', while the body says 7.1% of 'India's GDP'. The recap uses the body wording; treat the 7.1% as needing care before quoting.
PM E-DRIVE outlay: the government factsheet reported by DD News (1 Oct 2026) says ₹11,900 crore; earlier reports and the launch coverage said ₹10,900 crore. Shown as ₹11,900 crore with this note.

Logistics cost as a share of GDP: a KPMG blog (Jan 2026) quotes recent government assessments of about 8%; another report (Business Standard, not opened) puts it near 10 to 10.7%; older figures were 13 to 14%. No single figure is shown.
notFound: Cumulative FDI into the automobile industry: a figure appeared in a search result, but the DPIIT factsheet could not be opened to confirm it, so it is not shown.
Total employment in the auto industry: a '30 million jobs' figure appeared only in a search snippet, so it is not shown.
